method:
*Hole in Space* (1980): Artists set up large screens and cameras in both New York and Los Angeles, allowing passersby in the two cities to see each other in real time—essentially "the first public Zoom." Bringing people from different locations into a shared space is a long-standing theme in art, predating its commercial application. "What kind of real-time experience could exist between China and the UK?"
Core technologies: Protocols such as packets, TCP, UDP, HTTP, WebSocket, and WebRTC are all utilized.
 Nothing on the internet is transmitted as a single, complete block; instead, everything is broken down into small "packets." These packets may arrive late, out of order, or get lost entirely.
TCP functions like a structured phone call: A browser pings GitHub—"Are you there?" → "Yes, what do you need?" → "Send me *index.html*" → "Here you go." If a packet is lost, the process pauses to request it again. The slow loading of complex websites is often due to this constant back-and-forth of requesting packets.
UDP is used for live streaming: It doesn't wait or ask questions; it simply keeps calling out, "Send me the next packet!" If a packet is lost, it’s ignored—the priority is the present moment (this is why a Zoom call might freeze or "jump" occasionally).
WebSocket: Instead of constant back-and-forth questioning, it maintains an open connection, allowing data to flow freely. A server acts as an intermediary: Site 1 sends data → the server decodes it → it is forwarded to Site 2, enabling two clients to communicate with each other. Zoom also uses a server as an intermediary.
related_work: Reading: E-book by Vilém Flusser—read the first few chapters: "To Abstract," "To Imagine," "To Make Concrete," and "To Touch." (Flusser is a media philosopher who explores dialogue and communication.) Based on the chapter titles, the text is *Into the Universe of Technical Images*; the link is available on BB.

results_discussion:
Shift your perspective from "creating content for a webpage" to "communicating with others through webpages." Project 1 is a "duet": two or more websites connect to each other’s real-time data to create a meaningful, dialogical experience. While Project 0 is a "broadcast" (I have an idea, a story, or an aesthetic—come and experience it), Project 1 is a "dialogue" (meaning emerges from the interaction between the two sites).
Data is the raw material of a webpage. Just as an architect decides where to place walls using bricks and glass, a web creator uses data—text, images, sound, video, tables, 3D models, code, or anything a machine can parse according to a specific structure—as its "bricks." A painting on a wall isn't "data" until it’s scanned into a digital format. Humans decode information using their senses and brains (e.g., smelling that milk has gone bad); computers work similarly—if you provide data that a machine cannot decode, it might as well not exist.
For every file, ask two questions: Can the browser read it? How heavy (large) is it? If a file is too heavy, it will cause the entire page to lag or freeze.
Encoding: Every character corresponds to a specific number (e.g., A=65, é=233, an emoji=128512). The set of rules mapping these is called "encoding," and the web standard is UTF-8. If the rules are misinterpreted, the content becomes garbled (this is especially common with Chinese characters; "CAFÉ" might turn into strange symbols, or a semicolon might be misread, causing JavaScript to throw an error). This is currently an issue on GitHub: it misidentifies a file's format, preventing it from being uploaded.
Plain text vs. packages: Formats like .html, .css, .csv, and .json are plain text and can be opened in any editor. Formats like .docx or .xlsx are "packages" (essentially a ZIP file containing a collection of XML files); browsers cannot read these directly and must "unpack" them first (which can be done via explicit JavaScript instructions).
Images: Raster images (bitmaps) consist of instructions for every individual pixel, which makes them large (a 4K image contains tens of millions of pixels). Vector images consist of instructions for drawing shapes (e.g., "draw a blue circle here"), requiring only a line or two of code. Adobe Illustrator creates vector graphics, and p5.js—which we will use this week—also relies on vector-based drawing. JPEG is easy to compress but is lossy and lacks transparency; PNG supports transparency but results in large file sizes; GIF, WebP, and SVG each serve specific purposes.
Audio: Involves thousands of samples per second. WAV is uncompressed and high-quality but large, while MP3 is compressed. Video is the most complex: a container (e.g., .mp4, .mov, .webm) holds video tracks, audio tracks, and timing information, while a codec determines how the content is compressed. For instance, using 8 frames per second instead of 30 for an animation is a matter of how that timing information is defined.
Compression = discarding information. Consider describing a classmate: saying "he is a human" is a poor form of compression (since everyone is human). A better approach—like describing a classmate to your mother—would be to mention their height, whether they wear glasses, their hairstyle, and your relationship to them; this is effective compression. Among classmates, simply saying "the one who sits in the front row" is sufficient, as both parties can decode the same context. JPEG works similarly: by stating "everything from here to here is blue," it discards subtle color variations—a worthwhile trade-off if the difference is imperceptible.
CSV: A table represented as text; the purpose of a table is to express relationships between data points (e.g., a car's color and price). Excel files are "containers" from which data must first be extracted. 3D formats: OBJ is an older, human-readable format (defining triangles via a collection of XYZ coordinates); FBX is a proprietary binary format from Autodesk, widely used in gaming; there are also GLTF and GLB. If software doesn't recognize a specific format, it simply cannot open the file.
JSON: A structured text format consisting of key-value pairs. It is human-readable and can be parsed by JavaScript with zero overhead. Most online communication happens via JSON, and it is also a powerful way to interact with AI. The content you enter into your portfolio backend each week is essentially JSON; the website reads that file and updates accordingly.
title: The Beginning of Project 1 and Learning p5.js
introduction: The first half of the session was dedicated to reviewing portfolio links, discussing Bristol (with a brief detour into point clouds and Gaussian splatting), and providing 30 minutes for students to catch up on their blogs. In the second half, we officially launched the new unit for Project 1: "Communication Technologies." We covered how data serves as the raw material for the web (encoding, file formats, and compression), followed by how data is transmitted between people (packets, TCP/UDP, and WebSockets). Project 1 is themed as a "duet"—two websites engaging in a "dialogue" using each other’s real-time data. I demonstrated a small project of my own: a two-person interactive experience where a camera tracks a user's face to control a digital avatar's expressions. We will be using p5.js, and our first p5.js workshop is scheduled for Wednesday.
